Surah 100: Al-ʿĀdiyāt (The Chargers). It is Medinan, and it has eleven verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿By the chargers, panting,﴾ ﴿and the strikers of sparks,﴾ ﴿and the raiders at dawn,﴾ ﴿stirring up dust thereby,﴾ ﴿and penetrating thereby into the midst of a gathering,﴾ ﴿indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is a witness to that,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth.﴾ ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered,﴾ ﴿and what is in the breasts is brought out,﴾ ﴿indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Aware of them?﴾

Al-ʿādiyāt (the chargers): those that run swiftly. It is a descriptive term, and the disagreement over what is described will come up in the tafsir. Al-ḍabḥ (panting): a loud sound made during intense running, which is neither neighing, nor bellowing, nor barking, but an unusual sound from an animal that pants. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that no animal pants except horses and dogs. It was said: this is not authentically reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, because camels pant too, and so do the black snakes, owls, the echo, the hare, the fox, and the bow, as the Arabs used ḍabḥ for them. Abū Ḥanīfah recited in describing a bow:
"A humming one of nashm or taʾallub, panting in the hand like the panting of a fox."
The lexicographers said: its original use is for the fox, and then it was borrowed for horses. It derives from ḍabaḥathu al-nār, meaning the fire changed its color without fully burning it; and inḍabaḥa lawnuhu means his color changed slightly toward blackness. Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-ḍabḥ and al-ḍabʿ mean intense running, and al-Mubarrad said likewise: ḍabḥ comes from the animal stretching its legs in its journey. Al-qadḥ (striking): striking, and it was said: extracting. From it comes qadaḥtu al-ʿayn, meaning I extracted the diseased matter from it; and al-qaddāḥ, al-qaddāḥah, and al-miqdaḥah are that by which fire is kindled. Aghāra ʿalā al-ʿaduww: he attacked the enemy seeking plunder, killing, or capture. Al-naqʿ (dust): the poet said:
"They come out from a scattered cloud of dust, bleeding, as if their ears were the tips of pens."
Ibn Rawāḥah said:
"May I lose my daughter if you do not see her stirring up dust from the two sides of Kudāʾ."
Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-naqʿ is raising the voice, and from it is Labīd's saying:
"So when a true cry rises, you milk them, with a jingling and clamor."
Al-kanūd (ungrateful): one who is ungrateful for blessings. The poet said:
"Ungrateful toward the blessings of men, and whoever is ungrateful toward the blessings of men will be far off."
From Ibn ʿAbbās: al-kanūd, in the language of Kindah and Ḥaḍramawt, means the disobedient; in the language of Rabīʿah and Muḍar, the ungrateful; in the language of Kinānah, the stingy of bad character. Muqātil said likewise, and al-Kalbī said the same, except that he said: in the language of Banū Mālik, the stingy; and he did not mention Ḥaḍramawt. It is said: kanada al-niʿmah kunūdan. Abū Zubayd said of the stingy:
"If you lose me, I will not be content with you, except that I am tested by a time of ingratitude."
Ḥaṣṣala al-shayʾ: he gathered it; it was also said: he distinguished it from others, and from it comes the saying al-miḥṣal for a sieve. Ḥaṣala al-shayʾ: it appeared and became clear.

﴿By the chargers, panting,﴾ ﴿and the strikers of sparks,﴾ ﴿and the raiders at dawn,﴾ ﴿stirring up dust thereby,﴾ ﴿and penetrating thereby into the midst of a gathering,﴾ ﴿indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is a witness to that,﴾ ﴿and indeed, he is intense in his love of wealth.﴾ ﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered,﴾ ﴿and what is in the breasts is brought out,﴾ ﴿indeed, their Lord, that Day, is fully Aware of them?﴾

This surah is Meccan according to Ibn Masʿūd, Jābir, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, and ʿAṭāʾ, and Medinan according to Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas, and Qatādah, because what precedes it contains a threat and warning of the Day of Resurrection, with reproach toward whoever does not prepare for that Day and who prefers the affairs of this world over the affairs of the Hereafter. "And the horses strive when they pant, into the basins of death, panting."
Abū ʿAbdullāh, ʿAlī, Ibrāhīm, al-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr said: al-ʿādiyāt are camels, by which God swears when they run from ʿArafah and from Muzdalifah when the pilgrims depart; and by the people of the Battle of Badr, when there were only two horses among them, one horse for al-Zubayr and one for al-Miqdad. By this ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, argued with Ibn ʿAbbās when they disputed, and Ibn ʿAbbās returned to ʿAlī's view, may God be pleased with them both. Ṣafiyyah bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib said:
"By the chargers on the morning of the gathering, with their hooves, when the dust rises."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: or by al-ʿādiyāt, as if it were said: and the panting ones, because panting occurs with running. End of quotation. If panting occurs with running, then the meaning of "al-ʿādiyāt" is not the meaning of "al-ḍābiḥāt," so it should not be interpreted by it.

﴿Fa-l-mūriyāt qadḥan﴾: al-īrāʾ is the bringing out of fire, meaning they strike stones with their hooves so that fire flies out from them as some stones strike others. It is said: qadaḥa fa-awrā, and qadaḥa fa-aṣlada. The fire that the hooves of horses or camels strike is called nār al-ḥubāḥib. The poet said:
"It cuts the Salūqī's double-woven fabric, and kindles with the flint the fire of al-ḥubāḥib."
It was also said: ﴿al-mūriyāt qadḥan﴾ is a metaphor or figure in the sense of horses that ignite war, said by Qatādah, and God said: ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 64]. It is said: "the oven has become hot" when war intensifies. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-mūriyāt are the group that schemes in war; the Arabs say this when they want to deceive a man: "By God, that will not happen, and I will certainly kindle it for you." And from him also: a band of raiders who light many fires to terrify. ʿIkrimah said: the tongues of men kindle fire from the greatness of what they speak, and display proofs and evidences, the manifesting of truth and the nullifying of falsehood. ﴿Fa-l-mughīrāt ṣubḥan﴾: meaning they raid the enemy at dawn. Whoever says they are camels says the Arabs say: aghāra when he runs swiftly. That is, from Muzdalifah to Minā, or at Badr. In this there is evidence that these attributes belong to one entity, since they are joined by fa-, which implies sequence. The apparent meaning is that they are the horses by which the unbelieving enemy is fought, and one cannot derive from the Battle of Badr that they are camels, even though there were only two horses there; because it is not mentioned that the cause of the revelation of this surah was the Battle of Badr, and after that it is hardly found that camels were used for fighting in God's way; rather, it is well known that fighting in God's way is done only with horses in the east and west of the lands.

﴿Fa-atharna﴾ is conjoined to the active participle that is the relative clause of al-, since it has the meaning of a verb, as its implied form is: those who ran, then raided, then stirred. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is conjoined to the verb that the active participle was placed in the position of. End of quotation. Our companions say: it is conjoined to the noun, since it has the meaning of a verb. The majority read ﴿fa-atharna﴾ and ﴿fa-wasaṭna﴾ with the letters thāʾ and sīn unstressed, while Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn Abī ʿAblah read them with the letters doubled; ʿAlī, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Laylā read only the sīn doubled. Al-Zamakhsharī said: Abū Ḥaywah read fa-atharna with doubling, in the sense of fa-aẓhirna bihi ghubāran, since "influence" in it carries the sense of "manifesting"; or he transposed thawarna into wathurna and changed the waw into a hamzah. It is also read: (fa-wassaṭna) with doubling for transitivity, and the bāʾ is added for emphasis, as in His saying: (fa-ʾtū bihi), and it is an intensification of wasaṭna. End of quotation. As for his saying "or he transposed," that is cold, far-fetched speculation; as for doubling being for transitivity, they have transmitted that wasaṭ, unstressed and stressed, has one meaning and that they are two dialects. The pronoun in bihi in the first case refers to the dawn, meaning they stirred up dust at that time; and bihi in the second case refers to the dawn; it was said: or to the dust, meaning they penetrated the dust into the gathering, so that wasaṭahu means their penetrating it. ʿAlī and ʿAbdullāh said: ﴿fa-wasaṭna bihi jamʿan﴾ means the camels, and "jamʿan" is a name for Muzdalifah, not a gathering of people. Bishr ibn Abī Ḥāzim said:
"They penetrated their gathering, and the one who fled escaped beneath the dust-cloud in the dark dust."
It was said: the pronoun in bihi, together, refers to the running implied by ﴿al-ʿādiyāt﴾ as well. It was also said: it refers to the place that the meaning requires, even though it has not been mentioned, because al-ʿādiyāt and what follows it indicate it. It was said: by al-naqʿ here is meant the shouting. The apparent meaning is that the sworn-by thing is the class of al-ʿādiyāt, and the al- in it is not for specific reference. The sworn-to thing is: ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. In a hadith: "The ungrateful one eats alone, withholds his gift, and beats his servant." Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan said: it is the one who denies God's blessing. From al-Ḥasan also: it is the one who blames his Lord, counting the misdeeds and forgetting the good deeds. Al-Fuḍayl said: it is the one whom a single misdeed causes to forget many good deeds, and who deals with God on a contract of exchange. ʿAṭāʾ said: (p-505) it is the one who does not give in calamities together with his people. It was said: the stingy. Ibn Qutaybah said: a kanūd land is one that grows nothing. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿wa-innahu﴾ refers to that, ﴿la-shahīd﴾: he witnesses to his ingratitude and cannot deny it, because his matter is manifest; this was said by al-Ḥasan and Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb. Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah said: it refers to God, meaning His Lord is a witness against him, and this is in the manner of a warning. Al-Tabrīzī said: it refers to God, and "His Lord is a witness against him" is the more correct view, because the pronoun must refer to the nearest of those mentioned, and this serves as a warning and deterrent from sins. End of quotation. Nearness is not preferred unless both are equal in meaning; here "al-insān" is the one spoken of, and the one to whom kanūd is attributed; moreover, the harmony of pronouns for one referent together with the soundness of meaning is preferable to making them refer to two different things, especially when the pronoun is placed between two pronouns referring to one. ﴿Wa-innahu﴾, that is, and indeed man ﴿li-ḥubbi al-khayr﴾, that is, for the love of wealth, ﴿la-shadīd﴾: he is strong in his love. It was said: he is stingy with wealth, restraining it. It is said of the stingy: shadīd and mutashaddid. Ṭarafah said:
"I see death taking away the noble and choosing the precious wealth of the vile, stingy one."
Qatādah said: wherever khayr occurs in the Qur'an, it means wealth. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is possible that this worldly good is meant, such as wealth, health, and rank with kings and the like, because the unbelievers and ignorant know nothing other than this; as for one who loves the good of the Hereafter, he is praised and hoped to succeed. Al-Farrāʾ said: the structure of the verse would be: "and indeed he is intensely loving of the good," and when love was mentioned first, he said "shadīd," omitting mention of love at the end, since it had already been mentioned, and for the sake of the verse-endings, like His saying: ﴿on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 18], where stormy belongs to the wind and not to the days, as if He had said: on a day of stormy wind. End of quotation. Others said something similar, since this is not its original construction; rather the lām in (li-ḥubbi) is the lām of cause, meaning: indeed he, because of love of wealth, is stingy; or: indeed he, because of love and preference for wealth, is strong and capable; and he, for love of the worship of God and thanking His blessings, is weak and sluggish. One says: he is strong for this matter and powerful for it when he is capable of it and in control of it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: or he meant: indeed he, for love of good things, is not open and expansive, but rather is strong and constricted.

Will he not know, when what is in the graves is scattered out? (Qur'an 100:9)

Note: this passage is part 2 of Abu Hayyan's commentary, so the translation below covers only the text given.

﴿أفَلا يَعْلَمُ﴾ is a rebuke (tawqif) directing the human being to consider his final destination, and the object of ya'lamu is omitted; it is the governing element of the adverbial clause (zarf), meaning: "Will he not know his final destination?" ﴿إذا بُعْثِرَ﴾ (when what is in the graves is scattered out).

Al-Hawfi said: idha is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by (idafa to) ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾, and its governing element is ya'lamu. End of quote. This is not clear, because the meaning is: "Does he not know now?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾ with the ʿayn, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it with the ḥa' (bu-ḥithra, i.e., ḥuthira). Al-Aswad ibn Zayd read (buḥitha, "was searched/examined"). Nasr ibn ʿAsim read (buḥthira) in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'dan read (wa-ḥaṣṣala) in the active voice, while the majority read it in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mar also, and Nasr ibn ʿAsim also, read (wa-ḥaṣala) in the active voice with a light ṣad. The meaning is that what is in the Mushaf (here: what is in the breasts/hearts, as applicable) is gathered together, i.e., it is brought out as collected and gathered; and it was said: it is distinguished and uncovered so that the recompense may fall upon it.

The majority read inna with a kasra on the hamza, (la-khabirun) with the lam: it is a resumptive statement (istithnaf ikhbar), and the governing element of (bihim) and of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ﴾ is the verb of recompense; He, exalted is He, is always All-Aware, but He has included in (khabir) the meaning of recompense for them on that Day. Abu al-Sammal and al-Hajjaj read it with a fatha on the hamza and without the lam. In this reading, the governance of ya'lamu over inna becomes apparent, but it is not possible to make (khabir) govern idha, because it is within the relative clause (silla) of the verbal inna; yet no governing element can be posited for it from the meaning of the sentence, since he said: "He recompenses them when it is scattered." On this assumption, it is permissible that ya'lamu be suspended from operating (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal) in the reading of the majority, and it has taken the place of the object of inna; and the lam in its predicate is evident, since it is in the position of an accusative governed by ya'lamu, and idha's governing element is drawn from the meaning of the sentence's content, its estimated form being: "As we said, He recompenses them when it is scattered."

Will he not know, when what is in the graves is scattered out? (Qur'an 100:9)

Note: this passage is part 2 of Abu Hayyan's commentary, so the translation below covers only the text given.

﴿أفَلا يَعْلَمُ﴾ is a rebuke (tawqif) directing the human being to consider his final destination, and the object of ya'lamu is omitted; it is the governing element of the adverbial clause (zarf), meaning: "Will he not know his final destination?" ﴿إذا بُعْثِرَ﴾ (when what is in the graves is scattered out).

Al-Hawfi said: idha is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by (idafa to) ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾, and its governing element is ya'lamu. End of quote. This is not clear, because the meaning is: "Does he not know now?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾ with the ʿayn, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it with the ḥa' (bu-ḥithra, i.e., ḥuthira). Al-Aswad ibn Zayd read (buḥitha, "was searched/examined"). Nasr ibn ʿAsim read (buḥthira) in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'dan read (wa-ḥaṣṣala) in the active voice, while the majority read it in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mar also, and Nasr ibn ʿAsim also, read (wa-ḥaṣala) in the active voice with a light ṣad. The meaning is that what is in the Mushaf (here: what is in the breasts/hearts, as applicable) is gathered together, i.e., it is brought out as collected and gathered; and it was said: it is distinguished and uncovered so that the recompense may fall upon it.

The majority read inna with a kasra on the hamza, (la-khabirun) with the lam: it is a resumptive statement (istithnaf ikhbar), and the governing element of (bihim) and of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ﴾ is the verb of recompense; He, exalted is He, is always All-Aware, but He has included in (khabir) the meaning of recompense for them on that Day. Abu al-Sammal and al-Hajjaj read it with a fatha on the hamza and without the lam. In this reading, the governance of ya'lamu over inna becomes apparent, but it is not possible to make (khabir) govern idha, because it is within the relative clause (silla) of the verbal inna; yet no governing element can be posited for it from the meaning of the sentence, since he said: "He recompenses them when it is scattered." On this assumption, it is permissible that ya'lamu be suspended from operating (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal) in the reading of the majority, and it has taken the place of the object of inna; and the lam in its predicate is evident, since it is in the position of an accusative governed by ya'lamu, and idha's governing element is drawn from the meaning of the sentence's content, its estimated form being: "As we said, He recompenses them when it is scattered."

One says: he is strong for this matter and powerful for it when he is capable of it and in control of it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: or he meant: indeed he, for love of good things, is not open and expansive, but rather is strong and constricted.

Will he not know, when what is in the graves is scattered out? (Qur'an 100:9)

Note: this passage is part 2 of Abu Hayyan's commentary, so the translation below covers only the text given.

﴿أفَلا يَعْلَمُ﴾ is a rebuke (tawqif) directing the human being to consider his final destination, and the object of ya'lamu is omitted; it is the governing element of the adverbial clause (zarf), meaning: "Will he not know his final destination?" ﴿إذا بُعْثِرَ﴾ (when what is in the graves is scattered out).

Al-Hawfi said: idha is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by (idafa to) ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾, and its governing element is ya'lamu. End of quote. This is not clear, because the meaning is: "Does he not know now?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾ with the ʿayn, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it with the ḥa' (bu-ḥithra, i.e., ḥuthira). Al-Aswad ibn Zayd read (buḥitha, "was searched/examined"). Nasr ibn ʿAsim read (buḥthira) in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'dan read (wa-ḥaṣṣala) in the active voice, while the majority read it in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mar also, and Nasr ibn ʿAsim also, read (wa-ḥaṣala) in the active voice with a light ṣad. The meaning is that what is in the Mushaf (here: what is in the breasts/hearts, as applicable) is gathered together, i.e., it is brought out as collected and gathered; and it was said: it is distinguished and uncovered so that the recompense may fall upon it.

The majority read inna with a kasra on the hamza, (la-khabirun) with the lam: it is a resumptive statement (istithnaf ikhbar), and the governing element of (bihim) and of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ﴾ is the verb of recompense; He, exalted is He, is always All-Aware, but He has included in (khabir) the meaning of recompense for them on that Day. Abu al-Sammal and al-Hajjaj read it with a fatha on the hamza and without the lam. In this reading, the governance of ya'lamu over inna becomes apparent, but it is not possible to make (khabir) govern idha, because it is within the relative clause (silla) of the verbal inna; yet no governing element can be posited for it from the meaning of the sentence, since he said: "He recompenses them when it is scattered." On this assumption, it is permissible that ya'lamu be suspended from operating (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal) in the reading of the majority, and it has taken the place of the object of inna; and the lam in its predicate is evident, since it is in the position of an accusative governed by ya'lamu, and idha's governing element is drawn from the meaning of the sentence's content, its estimated form being: "As we said, He recompenses them when it is scattered."

Note: this passage is part 2 of Abu Hayyan's commentary, so the translation below covers only the text given.

Al-Hawfi said: idha is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by (idafa to) ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾, and its governing element is ya'lamu. End of quote. This is not clear, because the meaning is: "Does he not know now?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾ with the ʿayn, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it with the ḥa' (bu-ḥithra, i.e., ḥuthira). Al-Aswad ibn Zayd read (buḥitha, "was searched/examined"). Nasr ibn ʿAsim read (buḥthira) in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'dan read (wa-ḥaṣṣala) in the active voice, while the majority read it in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mar also, and Nasr ibn ʿAsim also, read (wa-ḥaṣala) in the active voice with a light ṣad. The meaning is that what is in the Mushaf (here: what is in the breasts/hearts, as applicable) is gathered together, i.e., it is brought out as collected and gathered; and it was said: it is distinguished and uncovered so that the recompense may fall upon it.

The majority read inna with a kasra on the hamza, (la-khabirun) with the lam: it is a resumptive statement (istithnaf ikhbar), and the governing element of (bihim) and of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ﴾ is the verb of recompense; He, exalted is He, is always All-Aware, but He has included in (khabir) the meaning of recompense for them on that Day. Abu al-Sammal and al-Hajjaj read it with a fatha on the hamza and without the lam. In this reading, the governance of ya'lamu over inna becomes apparent, but it is not possible to make (khabir) govern idha, because it is within the relative clause (silla) of the verbal inna; yet no governing element can be posited for it from the meaning of the sentence, since he said: "He recompenses them when it is scattered." On this assumption, it is permissible that ya'lamu be suspended from operating (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal) in the reading of the majority, and it has taken the place of the object of inna; and the lam in its predicate is evident, since it is in the position of an accusative governed by ya'lamu, and idha's governing element is drawn from the meaning of the sentence's content, its estimated form being: "As we said, He recompenses them when it is scattered."

Al-Farrāʾ said: the structure of the verse would be: "and indeed he is intensely loving of the good," and when love was mentioned first, he said "shadīd," omitting mention of love at the end, since it had already been mentioned, and for the sake of the verse-endings, like His saying: ﴿on a stormy day﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 18], where stormy belongs to the wind and not to the days, as if He had said: on a day of stormy wind. End of quotation. Others said something similar, since this is not its original construction; rather the lām in (li-ḥubbi) is the lām of cause, meaning: indeed he, because of love of wealth, is stingy; or: indeed he, because of love and preference for wealth, is strong and capable; and he, for love of the worship of God and thanking His blessings, is weak and sluggish. One says: he is strong for this matter and powerful for it when he is capable of it and in control of it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: or he meant: indeed he, for love of good things, is not open and expansive, but rather is strong and constricted.

Will he not know, when what is in the graves is scattered out? (Qur'an 100:9)

Note: this passage is part 2 of Abu Hayyan's commentary, so the translation below covers only the text given.

﴿أفَلا يَعْلَمُ﴾ is a rebuke (tawqif) directing the human being to consider his final destination, and the object of ya'lamu is omitted; it is the governing element of the adverbial clause (zarf), meaning: "Will he not know his final destination?" ﴿إذا بُعْثِرَ﴾ (when what is in the graves is scattered out).

Al-Hawfi said: idha is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by (idafa to) ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾, and its governing element is ya'lamu. End of quote. This is not clear, because the meaning is: "Does he not know now?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿بُعْثِرَ﴾ with the ʿayn, in the passive voice (mabniyyan lil-maf'ul). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read it with the ḥa' (bu-ḥithra, i.e., ḥuthira). Al-Aswad ibn Zayd read (buḥitha, "was searched/examined"). Nasr ibn ʿAsim read (buḥthira) in the active voice (mabniyyan lil-fa'il). Ibn Ya'mar, Nasr ibn ʿAsim and Muhammad ibn Abi Sa'dan read (wa-ḥaṣṣala) in the active voice, while the majority read it in the passive voice. Ibn Ya'mar also, and Nasr ibn ʿAsim also, read (wa-ḥaṣala) in the active voice with a light ṣad. The meaning is that what is in the Mushaf (here: what is in the breasts/hearts, as applicable) is gathered together, i.e., it is brought out as collected and gathered; and it was said: it is distinguished and uncovered so that the recompense may fall upon it.

The majority read inna with a kasra on the hamza, (la-khabirun) with the lam: it is a resumptive statement (istithnaf ikhbar), and the governing element of (bihim) and of ﴿يَوْمَئِذٍ لَخَبِيرٌ﴾ is the verb of recompense; He, exalted is He, is always All-Aware, but He has included in (khabir) the meaning of recompense for them on that Day. Abu al-Sammal and al-Hajjaj read it with a fatha on the hamza and without the lam. In this reading, the governance of ya'lamu over inna becomes apparent, but it is not possible to make (khabir) govern idha, because it is within the relative clause (silla) of the verbal inna; yet no governing element can be posited for it from the meaning of the sentence, since he said: "He recompenses them when it is scattered." On this assumption, it is permissible that ya'lamu be suspended from operating (mu'allaqa 'an al-'amal) in the reading of the majority, and it has taken the place of the object of inna; and the lam in its predicate is evident, since it is in the position of an accusative governed by ya'lamu, and idha's governing element is drawn from the meaning of the sentence's content, its estimated form being: "As we said, He recompenses them when it is scattered."
